modern_osis:
Original heading

The safety of the godly.

Our help comes from the Lord

We must not put ultimate trust in human beings, methods, tools or secondary causes.

Should I depend upon the strength of the hills, on rulers or on powerful people?

No. My confidence is in God alone.

Or perhaps we are being called to look beyond the hills to the God who gives all earthly things their place and value.

All our help comes from him.

We should expect it from him in his own way and time.

This psalm teaches us to find comfort in the Lord especially when danger and difficulty are greatest.

His almighty wisdom plans the safety of those who place themselves under his care, and his almighty power accomplishes it.

He is a watchful Keeper.

He never tires, sleeps or even grows drowsy.

We may rest under his shelter with joy and confidence.

He is always near his people to protect and refresh them.

Our right hand represents our working hand.

When we turn toward the duties he has given us, we may find him ready to grant us success.

He guards his people from being finally overthrown.

Neither open attacks nor secret plots can cause them ultimate harm.

The Lord may prevent the trouble they fear or sanctify, remove or lessen the suffering they experience.

Above all, he protects their souls from sin's pollution, from being crushed under trials and from eternal destruction.

He watches over believers during life and death.

He is with them when they go out to work in the morning of life and when they return to rest in life's evening.

The Holy Spirit, their Preserver and Comforter, stays with them forever.

Let us therefore remain faithful in our work, confident in the blessing promised here.
classic_reading:
[Ps.121.1]
Chapter 121
The safety of the godly.
--We must not rely upon men and means, instruments and second causes. Shall I depend upon the strength of the hills? upon princes and great men? No; my confidence is in God only. Or, we must lift up our eyes above the hills; we must look to God who makes all earthly things to us what they are. We must see all our help in God; from him we must expect it, in his own way and time. This psalm teaches us to comfort ourselves in the Lord, when difficulties and dangers are greatest. It is almighty wisdom that contrives, and almighty power that works the safety of those that put themselves under God's protection. He is a wakeful, watchful Keeper; he is never weary; he not only does not sleep, but he does not so much as slumber. Under this shade they may sit with delight and assurance. He is always near his people for their protection and refreshment. The right hand is the working hand; let them but turn to their duty, and they shall find God ready to give them success. He will take care that his people shall not fall. Thou shalt not be hurt, neither by the open assaults, nor by the secret attempts of thine enemies. The Lord shall prevent the evil thou fearest, and sanctify, remove, or lighten the evil thou feelest. He will preserve the soul, that it be not defiled by sin, and disturbed by affliction; he will preserve it from perishing eternally. He will keep thee in life and death; going out to thy labour in the morning of thy days, and coming home to thy rest when the evening of old age calls thee in. It is a protection for life. The Spirit, who is their Preserver and Comforter, shall abide with them for ever. Let us be found in our work, assured that the blessings promised in this psalm are ours.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesEsteem for Jerusalem.1–5Concern for its welfare.6–9
Rejoicing in the gathering of God's people (verses 1–5)

The pleasure and benefit we receive through God's means of grace should make us willing to endure inconvenience and tiredness in order to attend them.

We should encourage one another toward what is good.

When Christian friends undertake some worthwhile work, we should want them to invite us and include us in it.

How eagerly should we look forward to the heavenly Jerusalem!

How cheerfully should we bear our cross and face death when we hope to receive a crown of glory!

Jerusalem is called a beautiful city.

It pictured the gospel church, whose members are joined together through holy love and Christian fellowship, making one united community.

If all Christ's disciples shared one mind and maintained the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, their enemies would lose many of their greatest advantages.

But Satan has always tried to divide in order to conquer, and too few Christians recognize his schemes.

Praying for Jerusalem's peace (verses 6–9)

Even those who cannot do anything else for Jerusalem's peace can pray.

We should regard all who sincerely seek the Redeemer's glory as brothers and sisters and fellow travelers, without allowing differences that do not affect eternal salvation to divide us.

Blessed Spirit of peace and love, who dwelt in the soul of the holy Jesus, come upon his church and fill its people with your heavenly character.

Put an end to bitter disputes and make us united in heart.

Love for fellow believers and love for God should move us to imitate Jesus through fervent prayer and tireless work for human salvation and God's glory.
classic_reading:
[Ps.122.1-Ps.122.5]
Chapter 122
Chapter Outline
Esteem for Jerusalem. | (1-5) |
Concern for its welfare. | (6-9) |
Verses 1-5
The pleasure and profit from means of grace, should make us disregard trouble and fatigue in going to them; and we should quicken one another to what is good. We should desire our Christian friends, when they have any good work in hand, to call for us, and take us with them. With what readiness should we think of the heavenly Jerusalem! How cheerfully should we bear the cross and welcome death, in hopes of a crown of glory! Jerusalem is called the beautiful city. It was a type of the gospel church, which is compact together in holy love and Christian communion, so that it is all as one city. If all the disciples of Christ were of one mind, and kept the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, their enemies would be deprived of their chief advantages against them. But Satan's maxim always has been, to divide that he may conquer; and few Christians are sufficiently aware of his designs.
[Ps.122.6-Ps.122.9]
Verses 6-9
Those who can do nothing else for the peace of Jerusalem, may pray for it. Let us consider all who seek the glory of the Redeemer, as our brethren and fellow-travellers, without regarding differences which do not affect our eternal welfare. Blessed Spirit of peace and love, who didst dwell in the soul of the holy Jesus, descend into his church, and fill those who compose it with his heavenly tempers; cause bitter contentions to cease, and make us to be of one mind. Love of the brethren and love to God, ought to stir us up to seek to be like the Lord Jesus in fervent prayer and unwearied labour, for the salvation of men, and the Divine glory.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Confidence in God under contempt.

Looking to our heavenly Master for mercy

Jesus taught us to approach God in prayer as our Father in heaven.

A godly person lifts the soul toward him in every prayer, especially when suffering.

We ask for mercy, trust he will grant it, and continue waiting until it comes.

Servants watch their master's hand for several reasons.

First, for direction: they expect him to assign their work.

Second, for provision: they look for the food they need at the right time.

Likewise, we look to God for daily bread and sufficient grace, receiving both with thanksgiving.

Third, for protection: if servants are mistreated while fulfilling their duties, their master should defend them.

Fourth, for correction: when we sin, we ought to turn humbly to the very One who has disciplined us, submitting under his mighty hand.

Finally, for reward: faithful servants look to their master's kindness.

Hypocrites look to the world's approval and receive the reward of worldly honor.

But genuine Christians regard God as both their Master and their Rewarder.

God's people may receive little mercy from other human beings.

Their comfort is that the Lord is full of mercy.

Mockery and contempt have always been, and will likely continue to be, part of the suffering of God's people.

It is difficult to endure.

Yet those who serve the Lord should not be surprised to receive treatment like that given to his beloved Son.

When suffering nearly overwhelms us, look to Jesus and entrust ourselves through faith and prayer to the mercy of God.
classic_reading:
[Ps.123.1]
Chapter 123
Confidence in God under contempt.
--Our Lord Jesus has taught us to look unto God in prayer as our Father in heaven. In every prayer a good man lifts up his soul to God; especially when in trouble. We desire mercy from him; we hope he will show us mercy, and we will continue waiting on him till it come. The eyes of a servant are to his master's directing hand, expecting that he will appoint him his work. And also to his supplying hand. Servants look to their master or their mistress for their portion of meat in due season. And to God we must look for daily bread, for grace sufficient; from him we must receive it thankfully. Where can we look for help but to our Master? And, further, to his protecting hand. If the servant is wronged and injured in his work, who should right him, but his master? And to his correcting hand. Whither should sinners turn but to him that smote them? They humble themselves under God's mighty hand. And lastly, to his rewarding hand. Hypocrites look to the world's hand, thence they have their reward; but true Christians look to God as their Master and their Rewarder. God's people find little mercy with men; but this is their comfort, that with the Lord there is mercy. Scorning and contempt have been, are, and are likely to be, the lot of God's people in this world. It is hard to bear; but the servants of God should not complain if they are treated as his beloved Son was. Let us then, when ready to faint under trials, look unto Jesus, and by faith and prayer cast ourselves upon the mercy of God.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe deliverance of the church.1–5Thankfulness for the deliverance.6–8
The Lord saves his people (verses 1–5)

Sometimes God allows his people's enemies to advance so far that his power is displayed more clearly when he rescues them.

Happy are those whose God is the Lord, the all-sufficient One.

We can apply this psalm to the deliverances he gave in ancient times or to rescues experienced in our own day.

But above all, let us remember the great redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ, through which believers were delivered from Satan's power.

All the glory belongs to God (verses 6–8)

God is the author of all our deliverances and deserves all the glory for them.

Enemies lay traps to draw his people into sin and trouble and then keep them there.

At times those plans appear to succeed.

Yet those who put their trust in the Lord will not ultimately be put to shame.

Believers credit their salvation entirely to God's power, mercy and faithfulness.

Looking back on his guidance, they respond with wonder and thanksgiving.

Let us rejoice that all our help for the future is in the One who made heaven and earth.
classic_reading:
[Ps.124.1-Ps.124.5]
Chapter 124
Chapter Outline
The deliverance of the church. | (1-5) |
Thankfulness for the deliverance. | (6-8) |
Verses 1-5
God suffers the enemies of his people sometimes to prevail very far against them, that his power may be seen the more in their deliverance. Happy the people whose God is Jehovah, a God all-sufficient. Besides applying this to any particular deliverance wrought in our days and the ancient times, we should have in our thoughts the great work of redemption by Jesus Christ, by which believers were rescued from Satan.
[Ps.124.6-Ps.124.8]
Verses 6-8
God is the Author of all our deliverances, and he must have the glory. The enemies lay snares for God's people, to bring them into sin and trouble, and to hold them there. Sometimes they seem to prevail; but in the Lord let us put our trust, and we shall not be put to confusion. The believer will ascribe all the honour of his salvation, to the power, mercy, and truth of God, and look back with wonder and thanksgiving on the way in which the Lord has led him. Let us rejoice that our help for the time to come is in him who made heaven and earth.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe security of the righteous.1–3Prayer for them, The ruin of the wicked.4, 5
A security stronger than mountains (verses 1–3)

Minds firmly resting upon God find true stability.

They are like Mount Zion, strong through Providence and even stronger through God's promise.

Those who trust him cannot finally be driven away from their confidence.

His grace within them is a pledge of their eternal life in glory.

Because they entrust themselves to God, they are safe from their enemies in the ultimate sense.

Even mountains eventually crumble and rocks are moved.

But God's covenant cannot be broken, and his care for his people cannot cease.

Their suffering will not exceed what the Lord enables them to bear.

Wicked people may strike believers and affect their bodies, property, freedoms, families and reputations.

But they cannot destroy the believer's soul.

Their oppression may reach the righteous person's earthly circumstances, but it will not remain there forever.

God will work all these things together for their good.

Wicked people become a rod of correction, not a sword of destruction.

Even that rod will eventually be removed, so that believers will not be left thinking God has abandoned them.

Prayer for the upright and warning to the crooked (verses 4 and 5)

God's promises should encourage our prayers.

The path of holiness is straight.

It does not twist and turn in dishonest compromises.

But the ways of sinners are crooked.

They change their purposes and use deceit to get what they want.

Disappointment and misery will eventually come upon them.

Those who remain on God's path may suffer along the way, but their final destination is peace.

Their Savior's intercession secures God's sustaining power and preserving grace for them.

Lord, count us among them now and for eternity.
classic_reading:
[Ps.125.1-Ps.125.3]
Chapter 125
Chapter Outline
The security of the righteous. | (1-3) |
Prayer for them, The ruin of the wicked. | (4-5) |
Verses 1-3
All those minds shall be truly stayed, that are stayed on God. They shall be as Mount Zion, firm as it is; a mountain supported by providence, much more as a holy mountain supported by promise. They cannot be removed from confidence in God. They abide for ever in that grace which is the earnest of their everlasting continuance in glory. Committing themselves to God, they shall be safe from their enemies. Even mountains may moulder and come to nothing, and rocks be removed, but God's covenant with his people cannot be broken, nor his care of them cease. Their troubles shall last no longer than their strength will bear them up under them. The rod of the wicked may come, may fall upon the righteous, upon their persons, their estates, their liberties, their families names, on any thing that falls to their lot; only it cannot reach their souls. And though it may come upon their lot, it shall not rest thereon. The Lord will make all work together for their good. The wicked shall only prove a correcting rod, not a destroying sword; even this rod shall not remain upon them, lest they distrust the promise, thinking God has cast them off.
[Ps.125.4-Ps.125.5]
Verses 4-5
God's promises should quicken our prayers. The way of holiness is straight; there are no windings or shiftings in it. But the ways of sinners are crooked. They shift from one purpose to another, and turn hither and thither to deceive; but disappointment and misery shall befal them. Those who cleave to the ways of God, though they may have trouble in their way, their end shall be peace. The pleading of their Saviour for them, secures to them the upholding power and preserving grace of their God. Lord, number us with them, in time, and to eternity.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThose returned out of captivity are to be thankful.1–3Those yet in captivity are encouraged.4–6
Thankfulness for deliverance (verses 1–3)

It is good to pay attention to God's deliverances of his church and to share in the joy those rescues bring.

How highly should we value the greater redemption that saves us from the coming judgment, the power of sin and Satan!

When a sinner becomes aware of guilt and danger, looks to the crucified Savior, receives peace of conscience and finds new strength to abandon sinful conduct, the change may be so wonderful that it hardly seems real.

Praying and sowing through tears (verses 4–6)

The beginnings of God's mercy encourage us to pray that he will complete what he has started.

As long as we remain in this world, there will always be something to pray for, even when we have abundant reasons for praise.

Suffering believers often cry.

They share the hardships of human life and commonly endure an even greater share than others.

Yet they sow while they weep.

They perform their duties even in a painful season.

Tears must not keep us from sowing.

We should seek spiritual benefit from times of suffering.

Those who sow to the Spirit, even amid tears of godly repentance, will from the Spirit reap eternal life.

What a joyful harvest that will be!

Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted forever.

When we grieve over sin or suffer for Christ, we are sowing in tears and will one day reap with joy.

Remember also that God cannot be mocked: we will reap what we sow (Galatians 6:7–9).

Disciple of Jesus, see here a picture of your present work and future reward.

The day is coming when your harvest will be abundant and your joy in the Lord will be great.
classic_reading:
[Ps.126.1-Ps.126.3]
Chapter 126
Chapter Outline
Those returned out of captivity are to be thankful. | (1-3) |
Those yet in captivity are encouraged. | (4-6) |
Verses 1-3
It is good to observe how God's deliverances of the church are for us, that we may rejoice in them. And how ought redemption from the wrath to come, from the power of sin and of Satan, to be valued! The sinner convinced of his guilt and danger, when by looking to a crucified Saviour he receives peace to his conscience, and power to break off his sins, often can scarcely believe that the prospect which opens to him is a reality.
[Ps.126.4-Ps.126.6]
Verses 4-6
The beginnings of mercies encourage us to pray for the completion of them. And while we are in this world there will be matter for prayer, even when we are most furnished with matter for praise. Suffering saints are often in tears; they share the calamities of human life, and commonly have a greater share than others. But they sow in tears; they do the duty of an afflicted state. Weeping must not hinder sowing; we must get good from times of affliction. And they that sow, in the tears of godly sorrow, to the Spirit, shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting; and that will be a joyful harvest indeed. Blessed are those that mourn, for they shall be for ever comforted. When we mourn for our sins, or suffer for Christ's sake, we are sowing in tears, to reap in joy. And remember that God is not mocked; for whatever a man soweth that shall he reap, [Gal.6.7-Gal.6.9] Ga 6:7-9. Here, O disciple of Jesus, behold an emblem of thy present labour and future reward; the day is coming when thou shalt reap in joy, plentiful shall be thy harvest, and great shall be thy joy in the Lord.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The value of the Divine blessing.

The Lord builds, protects and provides

We must continually recognize God's Providence.

In every matter affecting a household, we depend upon his blessing.

Henry describes three areas.

First, establishing a family.

If we do not recognize God, we have no reason to expect his help.

Even the most carefully made plans fail unless he grants success.

Second, protecting a family or city.

Unless the Lord guards the city, watchmen keep watch in vain, even if they never sleep.

Danger may arise that no amount of early detection can prevent.

Third, providing for a family's needs.

Some people pursue money so eagerly that their continual worry makes every comfort bitter and turns life into a burden.

They labor to acquire wealth, yet all their efforts are vain unless God prospers them.

Those who love the Lord, act diligently in lawful work and entrust their cares to him may receive what is needed without being consumed by anxiety.

We should seek to remain in God's love and be content whether we possess little or much.

But this never excuses laziness: we must use appropriate means diligently.

Children are gifts from God, a heritage and reward.

They should be counted as blessings rather than burdens.

We can trust that the One who gives children can also provide for their needs.

Children may become a source of strength and defense for the household.

When they are young, parents can direct them like arrows toward a target—God's glory and the good of their generation.

Once children have gone out into the world, they are arrows released from the hand; their earlier direction can no longer be changed in the same way.

Yet arrows in the hand can also become arrows in the heart, bringing pain to godly parents.

When children are raised according to God's word, however, they generally offer valuable support later in life.

They remember what their parents have done for them and care for them in old age.

All earthly comforts remain uncertain.

Yet the Lord will surely comfort and bless those who serve him.

And those who labor for the conversion of sinners will find that their spiritual children are their joy and crown at the day of Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Ps.127.1]
Chapter 127
The value of the Divine blessing.
--Let us always look to God's providence. In all the affairs and business of a family we must depend upon his blessing. 1. For raising a family. If God be not acknowledged, we have no reason to expect his blessing; and the best-laid plans fail, unless he crowns them with success. 2. For the safety of a family or a city. Except the Lord keep the city, the watchmen, though they neither slumber nor sleep, wake but in vain; mischief may break out, which even early discoveries may not be able to prevent. 3. For enriching a family. Some are so eager upon the world, that they are continually full of care, which makes their comforts bitter, and their lives a burden. All this is to get money; but all in vain, except God prosper them: while those who love the Lord, using due diligence in their lawful callings, and casting all their care upon him, have needful success, without uneasiness or vexation. Our care must be to keep ourselves in the love of God; then we may be easy, whether we have little or much of this world. But we must use the proper means very diligently. Children are God's gifts, a heritage, and a reward; and are to be accounted blessings, and not burdens: he who sends mouths, will send meat, if we trust in him. They are a great support and defence to a family. Children who are young, may be directed aright to the mark, God's glory, and the service of their generation; but when they are gone into the world, they are arrows out of the hand, it is too late to direct them then. But these arrows in the hand too often prove arrows in the heart, a grief to godly parents. Yet, if trained according to God's word, they generally prove the best defence in declining years, remembering their obligations to their parents, and taking care of them in old age. All earthly comforts are uncertain, but the Lord will assuredly comfort and bless those who serve him; and those who seek the conversion of sinners, will find that their spiritual children are their joy and crown in the day of Jesus Christ.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The blessings of those who fear God.

The happiness of those who walk in God's ways

Only people who are truly devoted to God are truly happy.

We cannot reasonably claim to fear him if we do not strive conscientiously to walk in his ways.

Everyone who reverences the Lord can be blessed—whether powerful or obscure, rich or poor.

If we fear him and walk in obedience, life will be good under his care; death will bring something better, and eternity the greatest happiness.

With God's blessing, the faithful can earn an honest living.

Henry sees a twofold promise here.

They will have worthwhile work to do, because idleness is miserable and joyless.

They will also be given the ability, bodily strength and mental capacity needed for the work.

They need not live by exploiting the labor of others.

Quietly working and eating our own bread is both a duty and a mercy.

They and their families may enjoy the results of that labor.

Those who fear the Lord and follow his ways are blessed regardless of social position.

They will find abundant comfort in their family relationships and receive the good things God has promised and for which they pray.

Yet a good person gains little lasting consolation from seeing grandchildren if there is no peace for Israel.

Every genuine believer rejoices in the welfare and growth of God's church.

Beyond this life we will see far greater blessings: the everlasting peace and rest reserved for God's Israel.
classic_reading:
[Ps.128.1]
Chapter 128
The blessings of those who fear God.
--Only those who are truly holy, are truly happy. In vain do we pretend to be of those that fear God, if we do not make conscience of keeping stedfastly to his ways. Blessed is every one that fears the Lord; whether he be high or low, rich or poor in the world. If thou fear him and walk in his ways, all shall be well with thee while thou livest, better when thou diest, best of all in eternity. By the blessing of God, the godly shall get an honest livelihood. Here is a double promise; they shall have something to do, for an idle life is a miserable, uncomfortable life, and shall have health and strength, and power of mind to do it. They shall not be forced to live upon the labours of other people. It is as much a mercy as a duty, with quietness to work and eat our own bread. They and theirs shall enjoy what they get. Such as fear the Lord and walk in his ways, are the only happy persons, whatever their station in life may be. They shall have abundant comfort in their family relations. And they shall have all the good things God has promised, and which they pray for. A good man can have little comfort in seeing his children's children, unless he sees peace upon Israel. Every true believer rejoices in the prosperity of the church. Hereafter we shall see greater things, with the everlasting peace and rest that remain for the Israel of God.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThankfulness for former deliverances.1–4A believing prospect of the destruction of the enemies of Zion.5–8
Remembering deliverance amid persecution (verses 1–4)

The enemies of God's people have often sought cruelly to wear down and destroy the saints of the Most High.

Yet the Lord has repeatedly delivered his church through grace.

Christ built his church upon a rock.

He has many ways of restraining evildoers and preventing them from accomplishing the harm they plan.

The Lord acts righteously when he refuses to allow his people to be completely destroyed, because he has promised to preserve a people for himself.

The fate of those opposing Zion (verses 5–8)

God's people can flourish like a fruit-bearing palm or green olive tree.

Their enemies, however, are like grass growing on rooftops.

In the lands described here, roofs were flat and the thin layer of soil allowed grass to grow briefly but never mature.

That is the future of schemes directed against God's people.

No wise person asks God to bless people engaged in such destructive work.

Remember that Jesus rose and now reigns.

Remember how his people have survived like the bush that burned but was not consumed.

Therefore, do not be overcome by fear.
classic_reading:
[Ps.129.1-Ps.129.4]
Chapter 129
Chapter Outline
Thankfulness for former deliverances. | (1-4) |
A believing prospect of the destruction of the enemies of Zion. | (5-8) |
Verses 1-4
The enemies of God's people have very barbarously endeavoured to wear out the saints of the Most High. But the church has been always graciously delivered. Christ has built his church upon a rock. And the Lord has many ways of disabling wicked men from doing the mischief they design against his church. The Lord is righteous in not suffering Israel to be ruined; he has promised to preserve a people to himself.
[Ps.129.5-Ps.129.8]
Verses 5-8
While God's people shall flourish as the loaded palm-tree, or the green and fruitful olive, their enemies shall wither as the grass upon the house-tops, which in eastern countries are flat, and what grows there never ripens; so it is with the designs of God's enemies. No wise man will pray the Lord to bless these mowers or reapers. And when we remember how Jesus arose and reigns; how his people have been supported, like the burning but unconsumed bush, we shall not fear.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe psalmist's hope in prayer.1–4His patience in hope.5–8
Crying to the God who forgives (verses 1–4)

A soul entangled in sin can find true relief only by turning to God.

Many amusements distract us, and many supposed remedies offer help.

But the soul discovers that the Lord alone can heal it.

Until we recognize our guilt and abandon our self-reliance to come directly to him, we will look in vain for peace.

The Holy Spirit awakens people to a fresh understanding of their deep need and moves them to earnest prayer in faith.

For their souls' welfare and God's glory, they must not neglect this duty.

Why do some continue in uncertainty for so long?

Often it is because laziness or discouragement makes them settle for merely routine, customary prayers.

Let us take action and seek the Lord.

We can approach him safely.

We must humble ourselves as guilty before God.

We cannot justify ourselves or claim innocence.

But what an inexpressible comfort that forgiveness is available with him, exactly what we need!

Jesus Christ is the great Ransom and our continual Advocate.

Through him we hope to receive pardon.

There is forgiveness with God not so that we can treat sin lightly, but so that we will fear and reverence him.

The fear of God often describes the whole life of worshiping him.

For sinners, the great invitation and encouragement is simply this: the Lord offers forgiveness.

Waiting for abundant redemption (verses 5–8)

My soul waits for the Lord himself, for the gifts of his grace and the work of his power.

We should hope only for what God has promised in his word.

A watchman longs for the morning light before day breaks.

In the same way, a godly soul waits even more eagerly for signs of the Lord's favor and renewed grace.

Everyone devoted to the Lord should remain confident in him.

This redemption delivers us from all sin.

Jesus Christ saves his people from their sins, removing both sin's condemnation and sin's power to command.

His redemption is abundant.

The Redeemer possesses a fullness sufficient for everyone and for each believer individually.

There is enough for me, too.

Freedom from sin includes freedom from every other evil that would finally destroy us.

Through Jesus' atoning blood, his people will be fully redeemed from all their sins.

Everyone who waits upon God for mercy and grace can look forward to peace.
classic_reading:
[Ps.130.1-Ps.130.4]
Chapter 130
Chapter Outline
The psalmist's hope in prayer. | (1-4) |
His patience in hope. | (5-8) |
Verses 1-4
The only way of relief for a sin-entangled soul, is by applying to God alone. Many things present themselves as diversions, many things offer themselves as remedies, but the soul finds that the Lord alone can heal. And until men are sensible of the guilt of sin, and quit all to come at once to God, it is in vain for them to expect any relief. The Holy Ghost gives to such poor souls a fresh sense of their deep necessity, to stir them up in earnest applications, by the prayer of faith, by crying to God. And as they love their souls, as they are concerned for the glory of the Lord, they are not to be wanting in this duty. Why is it that these matters are so long uncertain with them? Is it not from sloth and despondency that they content themselves with common and customary applications to God? Then let us up and be doing; it must be done, and it is attended with safety. We are to humble ourselves before God, as guilty in his sight. Let us acknowledge our sinfulness; we cannot justify ourselves, or plead not guilty. It is our unspeakable comfort that there is forgiveness with him, for that is what we need. Jesus Christ is the great Ransom; he is ever an Advocate for us, and through him we hope to obtain forgiveness. There is forgiveness with thee, not that thou mayest be presumed upon, but that thou mayest be feared. The fear of God often is put for the whole worship of God. The only motive and encouragement for sinners is this, that there is forgiveness with the Lord.
[Ps.130.5-Ps.130.8]
Verses 5-8
It is for the Lord that my soul waits, for the gifts of his grace, and the working of his power. We must hope for that only which he has promised in his word. Like those who wish to see the dawn, being very desirous that light would come long before day; but still more earnestly does a good man long for the tokens of God's favour, and the visits of his grace. Let all that devote themselves to the Lord, cheerfully stay themselves on him. This redemption is redemption from all sin. Jesus Christ saves his people from their sins, both from the condemning and from the commanding power of sin. It is plenteous redemption; there is an all-sufficient fulness in the Redeemer, enough for all, enough for each; therefore enough for me, says the believer. Redemption from sin includes redemption from all other evils, therefore it is a plenteous redemption, through the atoning blood of Jesus, who shall redeem his people from all their sins. All that wait on God for mercy and grace, are sure to have peace.
